items.why: The negation distinguishes failing to change from appointing priests again.
It requires separating the original declarer from the prophet retelling it, but “gives” is ambiguous.
The summary assigns all four deaths to David and his men, not solely to Jonathan.
Pronoun resolution through the fulfilled prediction identifies the officer, not the man of God.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet is the one who mounts it.
“First covenant” selects the three-party covenant rather than the following two-party one.
The chronology places Jotham’s succession after the burial and Isaiah’s record earlier.
The explicit because-clause gives divine affliction, not the priests’ concurrent action, as the cause.
The nested plan orders leaving camp, capturing people, and then entering the city.
The men reject entering the city and instead choose the Aramean camp.
The ordering of two battles makes Sibbekai the first killer mentioned.
The report refers to the news, though the question’s generic wording weakens uniqueness.
The command’s object pronoun refers to the man of God, not the speaking king.
The object of “followed” is Uzziah, while Azariah leads the following priests.
Correctly mapping the two women and the quoted plan places the other child on tomorrow.
Zechariah instructs Uzziah, whereas Amaziah is only the model for his conduct.
“In reply to the doubt” selects Elisha’s second statement rather than his initial price prophecy.
The stated cause is the Lord’s command, not the amount of the king’s offer.
The event sequence puts prolonged talking directly before Paul’s departure.
The verb sequence places mobilizing the army before marching and laying siege.
The pronoun denotes Jehoiada as giver despite David being the weapons’ former owner.
The accusers receive the order; the Sanhedrin is only the earlier hearing venue.
The purpose clause is making Uzziah king, while Amaziah’s death is background circumstance.
“Under their command” refers to the 2,600 family leaders, not the officials who mustered the army.
Resolving the shifting pronouns shows the traveling man of God, not the old prophet, meets the lion.
The officer assigned to the gate is the one trampled there, not the king.
The instruction assigns temple protection specifically to the two off-duty companies, not the three on duty.
The letter heading distinguishes Claudius Lysias as sender from Felix as addressee.
The rescue relation makes Ishbi-Benob the object of Abishai’s attack, not David.
After admitting wrongdoing, the men propose reporting immediately rather than repeating their earlier hiding.
Within Paul’s quoted instruction, the young man is the one with information.
The messengers’ return and report directly precede the people’s plundering.
The singular pronoun refers back to Uzziah, not to the plural field workers.
Tracking “my son” identifies the speaking woman’s child as the one eaten first.
The king requests prayer, but the man of God performs the intercession.
The enemies God helps against are separated from the Ammonites, who instead bring tribute.
The body is taken to the prophet’s city before it is placed in his tomb.
Joash is the hidden son accompanied by his nurse; Ahaziah is his dead father.
The explicit because-clause attributes the calm to Athaliah’s death, not the people’s rejoicing.
The two centurions receive the order, while the soldiers are part of what they must prepare.
The Arameans treat the Hittite and Egyptian kings as attackers and Israel’s king as their hirer.
The murderer is the messenger’s master who sent him—the king—not the messenger himself.
The embedded command’s pronouns designate the man of God as the invited eater.
The causal clause ties Paul’s long speech to his intended departure, not to the lamps.
The contrast sends the cavalry onward while the remaining soldiers return to the barracks.
The man attacks “them,” and the resulting “they” who flee are Sceva’s sons.
The predicate distinguishes illnesses being cured from evil spirits leaving the people.
The Sanhedrin petitions, but the commander is expected to bring Paul before it.
The sequence places public burning immediately after the scrolls are assembled.
The imperative targets anyone following the woman, while her own execution is narrated separately.
Hearing the noise motivates Athaliah’s movement; seeing the king occurs only afterward.
The ambushers are explicitly waiting for the commander’s consent as their trigger.
The old prophet directly addresses the man of God with the warning about “your body.”
Inside the prophecy, the future son Josiah is the agent who will sacrifice the priests.
